newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria detains S. Leone rebel leader - ambassador.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria detains S. Leone rebel leader - ambassador.

text.p: Nigeria detained Sierra Leone's rebel leader Foday Sankoh after he turned up on a private visit in possession of a pistol and ammunition, Nigeria's ambassador to Sierra Leone said on Wednesday.

Alhaji Mohamed Abubakar told Reuters that Sankoh was under house arrest in Lagos where he was taken after 15 hours of questioning by the security forces. Officials in Ivory Coast, Sankoh's hosts for most of the past year, confirmed the report.

"Corporal Foday Sankoh was held in Nigeria by security forces for entering into the country with a pistol and ammunition," the ambassador said. "He was taken to Lagos where he is now under house arrest."

Officials in Lagos said on Tuesday that Sankoh was staying at a government guest house and denied a report by the opposition National Concord newspaper on Friday, saying that Sankoh had been arrested. They said he had arrived on March 2.
The ambassador said that restrictions had been placed on Sankoh. "While in house arrest, Sankoh is not allowed to talk politics and has no privilege to telephone or any other means of communication."

Sankoh and his Revolutionary United Front took up arms in 1991. He and President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who took office a year ago after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, signed a peace deal in Ivory Coast on November 30.
Implementation of the peace deal has dragged suggesting that it was unravelling. Each side has accused the other of ceasefire violations.
Ivory Coast brokered the deal and Sankoh has spent most of the past year living there.

The ambassador expressed confidence that Sierra Leone's peace process would take hold. "Nigeria is in no doubt that the peace accord in Sierra Leone has come to stay and there is no way RUF intransigence will take Sierra Leone back from peace."
Nigeria, the regional power in West Africa, has a battalion of troops in Sierra Leone. They helped to protect installations in the capital Freetown during the war.
The two countries, both former British colonies, signed a new military training cooperation agreement on March 7.
"We have been training their forces since 1994 under an agreement that expired last year," a defence official in Nigeria said, adding that the new deal expanded on the old one.
